title: Decimals that neither terminate nor repeat
competency: Find and compare square roots, recognise irrational numbers and locate √2 on the number line.

keywords.def: A number that is an integer times itself: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, …
y is a square root of x if y² = x. The positive one is written √x.
A decimal that neither ends nor repeats, such as √2 or π. It cannot be written as a/b.

en.text: A perfect square is an integer times itself, like 9 = 3². A square root of x is a number whose square is x. Both 5 and −5 are square roots of 25. The sign √ means the positive root. If a < b, then √a < √b.

am.text: ፍጹም ካሬ ኢንቲጀር በራሱ ሲባዛ ነው፤ ለምሳሌ 9 = 3²። የx ካሬ ሥር ካሬው x የሆነ ቁጥር ነው። 5 እና −5 ሁለቱም የ25 ካሬ ሥሮች ናቸው። √ ምልክቱ አዎንታዊውን ሥር ያሳያል። a < b ከሆነ √a < √b ነው።

screens.title: A square of area 2
screens.text: A square has area 2 cm². Its side is s cm. A square of side 1 has area 1. A square of side 2 has area 4.
screens.ask: How long do you think the side s is?
screens.after:
Side 1 gives area 1, too small.
Side 2 gives area 4, too big.
Area 2 is between 1 and 4, so s is between 1 and 2.
Read on to squeeze s closer and closer.

screens.title: Perfect squares and square roots
paras: A perfect square is an integer times itself: 1 = 1², 4 = 2², 9 = 3², …
A square root of x is a number y with y² = x.
For example, 5 and −5 are square roots of 25. This is because 5² = (−5)² = 25.

screens.title: Trapping the side s
paras: Since 1² = 1 and 2² = 4, s is between 1 and 2.
Squeeze further: 1.4² < 2 < 1.5², so 1.4 < s < 1.5.
Then 1.41 < s < 1.42, then 1.414 < s < 1.415, and so on.
We write s = √2 = 1.414… The sign √ is the radical sign.
screens.note: Each extra decimal place squeezes √2 into an interval ten times smaller. The digits never end or repeat.

screens.title: Squeeze the side of a square with area 2
screens.ask: Move the slider. Try to make the area as close to 2 as you can.

screens.title: Name it
defs: y is a square root of x when y² = x. √x is the positive one.

screens.title: Square roots of 25
screens.text: Square roots: which numbers are square roots of 25?
screens.why:
y is a square root of 25 when y² = 25.
5² = 5 × 5 = 25.
(−5)² = (−5) × (−5) = 25 too.
So 5 and −5 are both square roots. (√25 = 5 is the positive one.)
12.5 is half of 25, not a square root.
screens.clue: Which numbers give 25 when you square them?

screens.text: Write each one without the radical sign.

screens.title: Comparing square roots
paras: A square of side √5 cm has area 5 cm².
A square of side √7 cm has area 7 cm².
The bigger square has the longer side, so √5 < √7.
If a > 0, b > 0 and a < b, then √a < √b. Example: 5 < 6, so √5 < √6.

screens.title: √11 or 3.5?
screens.text: Comparing square roots: which is larger, √11 or 3.5?

screens.title: Without the radical
screens.why:
Look for a number whose square is 0.09.
3 × 3 = 9, and 0.3 × 0.3 has 1 + 1 = 2 decimal places.
So 0.3² = 0.09.
So √0.09 = 0.3 = 3/10.

screens.title: A square teff plot
screens.text: A farmer near Debre Markos has a square teff plot. Its area is 400 m².
screens.ask: Square root in a word problem: each side is ___ m long.
screens.why:
For a square, side × side = area.
So side² = 400 and side = √400.
20 × 20 = 400.
So each side is 20 m.
screens.worked: Side × side = 400. Try 20: 20 × 20 = 400. So each side is √400 = 20 m.

screens.title: Grow the tree for 324, then type √324.
screens.clue: Share the primes into two equal groups. Multiply one group.

en.text: Terminating and repeating decimals are rational. A decimal that neither ends nor repeats is irrational. If a natural number a is not a perfect square, √a is irrational. π is irrational too. We can still mark √2 exactly on the number line using a right triangle with legs 1 and 1.

am.text: የሚያልቁና የሚደጋገሙ አስርዮሾች ምክንያታዊ ናቸው። የማያልቅም የማይደጋገምም አስርዮሽ ኢ-ምክንያታዊ ነው። a የተፈጥሮ ቁጥር ሆኖ ፍጹም ካሬ ካልሆነ √a ኢ-ምክንያታዊ ነው። π ደግሞ ኢ-ምክንያታዊ ነው። ጎኖቹ 1 እና 1 የሆነ ቀኝ ማዕዘን ሦስት ማዕዘን በመጠቀም √2ን በቁጥር መስመር ላይ በትክክል ማመልከት እንችላለን።

screens.title: Does the calculator lie?
screens.text: A calculator shows √2 ≈ 1.4142135624. The screen is now full.
screens.ask: What do you think happens after the last digit?
opts: More digits follow, with no pattern
screens.after:
The calculator stops only because its screen is full.
More digits follow: 1.41421356237…
They never end and never repeat.
Read on to find out why.
screens.best: More digits follow, with no pattern

screens.title: Square roots that are not whole
paras: The calculator stops only because its screen is full.
The true decimal neither ends nor repeats. So √2 is not rational.
√3 and √7 behave the same way.

screens.title: Definition 1.6
paras: A decimal that is neither terminating nor repeating is an irrational number.
Remark. If a is a natural number that is not a perfect square, then √a is irrational.

screens.title: Name it
defs: A decimal that neither terminates nor repeats, such as √2 or π.

screens.title: Spot the irrational
screens.text: Irrational numbers: which number is irrational?
screens.why:
√49 = 7 and √0.25 = 0.5: rational.
0.333… repeats, so it is rational (1/3).
12 is not a perfect square: 3² = 9 < 12 < 16 = 4².
So √12 ≈ 3.464… neither ends nor repeats. √12 is irrational.
screens.clue: Which number under the √ is not a perfect square?

screens.title: Example: rational or irrational?
paras: (a) √25 = 5: rational. (b) √0.09 = 0.3: rational.
(c) 0.123456789101112… lists the counting numbers in a row. It neither terminates nor repeats, so it is irrational.
(d) 0.010110111…: irrational. (e) 22/7: a fraction, so rational. (f) π = 3.1415926…: irrational.
Parts (c), (d) and (f) show that such decimals really exist.
screens.note: Correction: the printed book writes "0.12345…" for (c) without saying how it continues. It then says "(a, b & d)" show non-repeating decimals. It is (c), (d) and (f); (a) and (b) are rational.

screens.title: 22/7 and π
screens.text: Rational or irrational: is 22/7 equal to π?
opts: No: 22/7 is rational and π is irrational
screens.ans: No: 22/7 is rational and π is irrational
screens.why:
22/7 is a fraction of integers, so it is rational.
As a decimal 22/7 = 3.142857142857…, which repeats.
π = 3.14159… neither ends nor repeats: it is irrational.
They differ from the third decimal place: 3.142… vs 3.141…
So 22/7 is only an approximation of π.

screens.title: Sort it
screens.text: Rational or irrational? Sort each number.
items: It is a fraction of integers.
Each block has one more 1, so it never repeats.
screens.why:
Rational numbers terminate or repeat. Irrational numbers do neither.
√25 = 5, √0.09 = 0.3, 22/7 and 0.2323… = 23/99: rational.
√7 and √18: 7 and 18 are not perfect squares, so irrational.
π and 0.010110111… never end or repeat: irrational.
screens.clue: Is the number under √ a perfect square? Does the decimal end or repeat?

screens.title: Locating √2 on the number line
paras: To mark √2 exactly, use a compass and straightedge.

screens.title: Square roots on the number line
screens.ask: Tap each point. The positions are rounded.

screens.title: Construct √2
steps: Draw a number line with 0 and 1 marked.
At 1, draw a segment of length 1 at right angles to the line.
Join 0 to the top of that segment. Call its length c.
Open the compass to length c. Put the point at 0. Draw an arc to cut the line at B. Then 0B = √2.
Repeat on top of the √2 segment to get √3, then √4 = 2, then √5.

screens.title: Why √2?
screens.text: Constructing √2: in the construction, why is the slanted line √2 long?
opts: Because the compass is opened to 2
Because it is twice as long as 1
screens.why:
The slanted line is the hypotenuse of a right triangle.
Both legs have length 1.
By Pythagoras: c² = 1² + 1² = 2.
So c = √2.
(It is not twice 1: 2 would be too long.)
screens.clue: Look at step 4 of the construction.

screens.title: A path across a field
screens.text: A school field in Hawassa is a square, 1 km on each side. Selam walks straight from one corner to the opposite corner.
screens.ask: Pythagoras and √2: her path is √___ km long.
screens.why:
The path is the diagonal of the square.
It is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 1 km and 1 km.
c² = 1² + 1² = 2.
So c = √2 km, about 1.414 km.
screens.clue: The path is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 1 and 1.
screens.worked: Legs 1 and 1. c² = 1² + 1² = 2. So c = √2 km, about 1.414 km.

items.why:
√25 is the positive number whose square is 25.
5 × 5 = 25.
So √25 = 5.

First find √36: 6 × 6 = 36, so √36 = 6.
The minus sign is outside the √.
So −√36 = −6.
items.clue: Find √36 first, then keep the minus sign.

items.why:
For positive a and b, a < b means √a < √b.
7 < 8.
So √7 < √8.

3 < 4, so √3 < √4 = 2.
Multiplying by −1 reverses the order.
So −√3 > −√4. (−1.73 is to the right of −2.)
items.clue: Which is further left on the number line?

items.why:
36 is a perfect square: 6 × 6 = 36.
So √36 = 6 = 6/1.
Rational.

7 is not a perfect square: 2² = 4 < 7 < 9 = 3².
By the Remark, √7 is irrational.
Its decimal 2.6457… never ends or repeats.

6/5 is a/b with integers a = 6, b = 5, and b ≠ 0.
As a decimal it is 1.2, which ends.
Rational.
items.clue: Is it a/b with integers a and b?

items.why:
13 is not a perfect square: 3² = 9 < 13 < 16 = 4².
So √13 is irrational.
A minus sign does not change that: −√13 is irrational.

18 is not a perfect square: 4² = 16 < 18 < 25 = 5².
By the Remark, √18 is irrational.
(Also √18 = √(9 × 2) = 3√2.)

items.text: 1(a) Locating square roots: between which two natural numbers is √3?
items.why:
Find perfect squares on each side of 3.
1 = 1² and 4 = 2², and 1 < 3 < 4.
So √1 < √3 < √4.
That is 1 < √3 < 2.
items.clue: Find the perfect squares on each side of 3.

items.text: 1(b) Locating square roots: between which two natural numbers is √5?
items.why:
Find perfect squares on each side of 5.
4 = 2² and 9 = 3², and 4 < 5 < 9.
So 2 < √5 < 3.
items.clue: Find the perfect squares on each side of 5.

items.text: 1(c) Locating square roots: between which two natural numbers is √6?
items.why:
Find perfect squares on each side of 6.
4 = 2² and 9 = 3², and 4 < 6 < 9.
So 2 < √6 < 3.
items.clue: Find the perfect squares on each side of 6.

items.text: 3(a) Points on the number line: every point on the number line is √n for some natural number n.
items.why:
√n is never negative.
So −1 is not √n for any n.
Also 1/2 = √(1/4), and 1/4 is not natural.
So not every point is √n. False.

items.text: 3(b) Irrational roots: the square root of every positive integer is irrational.
items.why:
Try a perfect square: 4 = 2².
√4 = 2, which is rational.
Only non-perfect squares give irrational roots.
So the statement is false.

test.text: Irrational numbers: which number is irrational?
test.why:
√16 = 4: rational.
0.5̅ = 5/9 and 7/3 are fractions: rational.
10 is not a perfect square (9 < 10 < 16).
So √10 neither ends nor repeats: irrational.

test.text: Locating square roots: √8 lies between 2 and 3.

notes.text: The printed book writes "0.12345…" for example (c) without saying how it continues, and then says "(a, b & d)" show non-repeating decimals. It is (c), (d) and (f) that show them; (a) and (b) are rational.
The printed book uses the label "Figure 1.6" twice: for the square-root construction and for the real-number diagram in lesson 1.4.
Exercise 1.17 (f) √11 and Exercise 1.18 Q2 (constructions with compass) are not turned into items.

screens.title: Square a decimal
screens.text: To square a number, multiply it by itself.
steps: (−5)² = (−5) × (−5) = 25. A negative times a negative is positive.

screens.title: Your turn
screens.why:
0.3² = 0.3 × 0.3.
First 3 × 3 = 9.
Count decimal places: 1 + 1 = 2.
So 0.3² = 0.09. (0.9 forgets one decimal place.)
screens.clue: Multiply 3 × 3, then count the decimal places.

screens.title: Rational numbers as decimals
screens.text: Divide a by b. One of two things happens.
steps: 3/5 = 0.6. The division stops: a terminating decimal.
5/9 = 0.555… The digits repeat: a repeating decimal.
Every fraction a/b gives one of these two kinds.

screens.title: Your turn
screens.text: Kinds of decimals: what kind of decimal is 1/3?
screens.why:
Divide 1 by 3: 10 ÷ 3 = 3 r 1.
The remainder 1 comes back every time.
So 1/3 = 0.333…
The 3 repeats for ever: a repeating decimal.

screens.title: Find the hypotenuse
screens.text: In a right triangle with legs a and b, the longest side c gives c² = a² + b².

screens.title: Your turn
screens.text: Pythagoras' theorem: a right triangle has legs 2 and 1. What is c²?
screens.why:
c² = a² + b².
2² = 4 and 1² = 1.
c² = 4 + 1 = 5.
So c² = 5 (and c = √5).
